data.text:
🚨💦🌊
The Hydrological Reality:

Manila Bay is not a sea. It is a semi-enclosed bay.

1. Manila Bay: A Semi-Enclosed Basin

Area: ~1,994 km² | Average depth: 17 m | Narrow entrance: 19 km

Water takes 2–4 weeks to circulate out — meaning floods linger.

Any blockage or reclamation affects the entire bay, even areas 20–30 km away.

---
2. “Basin Bowl Effect” (Habagat + High Tide + Reclamation + Storm Surge)

Monsoon winds push seawater inward; high tide lifts the water level further.
But the bay’s semi-enclosed shape and new reclamations trap the water —
forcing it back up the rivers, drowning Hagonoy, Calumpit, Paombong, Bulakan, Masantol, Macabebe, Valenzuela, and Malabon.

---
3. Two Giant River Systems

Pampanga River Basin

2nd largest in Luzon.

Drains Nueva Ecija, Tarlac, Pampanga, and Bulacan and bonus: upland sources in Nueva Vizcaya and Aurora.

All floodwaters eventually exit through Hagonoy, Calumpit, Masantol, and Macabebe into Manila Bay.

Meycauayan–Marilao–Obando River System (MMORS)

Final outlet for runoff from Balagtas, Guiguinto, Bocaue, Marilao, Meycauayan, and Valenzuela.

Has a dendritic drainage pattern — like tree roots converging into one main outlet to the bay.

---
4. NMIA Sits Between These Two Systems

The New Manila International Airport (NMIA) in Taliptip–Bambang, Bulakan lies right between the Pampanga and Meycauayan basins —
in what used to be a natural outlet zone with rivers and wetlands (Maycapiz, Taliptip, Bambang).

These have now been filled and reclaimed, erasing the natural flood buffer.

---
5. The Consequences

1. Bottleneck Effect – The reclaimed airport blocks the shared drainage path to Manila Bay, causing water from both basins to back up and flood inland longer.

2. Amplified Flooding – When rain, monsoon, and high tide coincide, water cannot escape; floods rise simultaneously across Bulacan, Pampanga, and CAMANAVA.  Distance doesn’t define impact — water connection does.

3. Loss of Wetlands – Natural “sponges” that once absorbed floodwater are gone, turning heavy rain directly into surface flooding.

---
The NMIA sits on the natural drain of Central Luzon.
Blocking that outlet doesn’t just endanger Bulakan — it worsens flooding for the entire Bulacan,Pampanga Delta and CAMANAVA floodplain.
